key_terms.meaning: Closeness of the measured value to the true value; error = measured − true.
Active sensor needs external power and modulates it; passive sensor takes energy from the measured quantity.
Analog sensor gives a continuous voltage or current; digital sensor gives discrete codes or pulses.
Uses C = εA/d, where ε is permittivity, A plate area and d gap; changes in d or ε give the signal.
Uses V_H = K_H I B, where I is current, B magnetic flux density and K_H sensitivity, to sense magnetic field.
Linear variable differential transformer; an AC output changes almost linearly with core displacement.
Output for increasing input differs from output for decreasing input at the same input value.
Slow change in output with time or temperature when the input is constant.
Range of input over which the output does not change.
Closed-loop motor with position or speed feedback; the controller drives it to a commanded value.
Motor that moves in fixed angular steps for each pulse; open-loop position is possible by counting steps.
Permanent-magnet motor with electronic commutation; efficient and long-lived but needs a driver.
Small package with sensing, processing, communication, power and identity that can report and act.
Node with sensor, microcontroller, radio and power source in a wireless sensor network.
Microcontroller or system-on-chip that reads sensors, runs logic and drives actuators.
One chip with CPU, memory, timers and input/output pins for deterministic low-power control.
Complete computer on one board with operating system, RAM, storage and ports, such as Raspberry Pi.
Many small nodes that sense, cooperate and pass data hop by hop to a sink.
Low-energy adaptive clustering hierarchy; rotates cluster heads to spread energy use in a WSN.
Chip plus antenna carrying an identity; a reader captures it by radio without contact or line of sight.

takeaways: Accuracy, drift, hysteresis and dead band decide whether a sensor reading can be trusted.
Active sensors need a power source; passive sensors convert energy from the measured quantity.
Analog sensors suit simple continuous measurement; digital sensors suit buses, noise immunity and microcontrollers.
An actuator type is chosen for position accuracy, speed, cost and feedback needs.
A servo closes the loop; a stepper counts steps; a BLDC gives efficient continuous motion.
A smart object is a sensor node plus local compute, identity and sometimes an actuator.
Control unit, communication module and power source must be selected together for an IoT device.
A microcontroller gives hard real-time control at low power; an SBC gives an OS and rich connectivity.
A WSN buys coverage with relay energy, so duty cycling and clustering decide network lifetime.
RFID supplies contactless identity, while sensors supply measurement; do not confuse the two.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to compare sensor or actuator types, justify hardware choices against power and communication limits, and explain WSN or RFID operation with a block diagram.

bank.q: Explain the static characteristics of a sensor: accuracy, precision, sensitivity, resolution, linearity, hysteresis, dead band and drift. Use one example for each.
outline: Define each characteristic in one line.
State error = measured − true for accuracy.
Give a practical example for each term.
Explain why static characteristics matter before dynamic response.

bank.q: Compare active and passive sensors, and analog and digital sensors. Give two practical examples of each type and state one advantage and one limit.
outline: Active sensor needs external power; passive sensor uses measured energy.
Analog output is continuous; digital output is discrete.
Examples such as thermistor, LDR, encoder and digital temperature sensor.
Advantages and limits for noise, interfacing and power.

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of an LVDT and a Hall effect sensor. State one industrial use of each.
outline: LVDT primary, two secondaries and movable core.
Output magnitude and phase indicate displacement direction.
Hall sensor uses V_H = K_H I B.
Uses: displacement measurement and magnetic position sensing.

bank.q: Explain the working of a DC servo motor, a variable-reluctance stepper motor and a brushless DC motor. State where each is preferred.
outline: Servo motor uses feedback and closed-loop control.
VR stepper moves by reluctance change and fixed steps.
BLDC uses electronic commutation and permanent magnets.
Applications: robot joint, printer head, drone or fan.

bank.q: Draw and explain the block diagram of a smart object and a sensor node. Mark sensing, processing, communication, power and identity.
outline: Sensor and signal conditioning block.
Processor or microcontroller block.
Radio and antenna block.
Power source and identity or ID block.
Difference between smart object and plain sensor node.

bank.q: A cold-chain truck must keep vaccines at 2 to 8 °C and log readings every minute. Select sensor characteristics and a control unit, and justify the communication and power choices.
outline: Required accuracy, resolution and drift.
Sensor placement and calibration.
MCU versus SBC choice.
Radio choice and battery or vehicle power.
Logging interval and alarm path.

bank.q: Design a room-monitoring IoT node with a temperature sensor, relay for a fan, Wi-Fi and a battery. Choose MCU or SBC, give a block diagram, and estimate the main power loads qualitatively.
outline: Sensor and relay interface.
MCU for deterministic control.
Wi-Fi module and antenna.
Battery and regulator.
Power loads: radio, processor, relay coil, sensor.

bank.q: Design a wireless sensor network for a 10-hectare drip-irrigated farm. Discuss node placement, coverage, LEACH clustering and duty cycling.
outline: Soil moisture and temperature nodes.
Coverage and connectivity plan.
LEACH cluster head rotation.
Duty cycling and sleep schedule.
Sink and backhaul to farm office.

bank.q: Apply RFID to a library issue-and-return desk. Compare passive and active tags, reader placement, and the data written on the tag.
outline: Tag ID and book metadata mapping.
Passive tag range and reader power.
Active tag cost and battery.
Reader placement at counter and exit.
Privacy and duplicate-read handling.

bank.q: Evaluate microcontroller versus single-board computer for a camera-based toll-gate reader. Discuss real-time response, power, cost, operating system and maintenance.
outline: MCU strengths: deterministic timing, low power.
SBC strengths: camera stack, OS, storage, networking.
Power and thermal limits.
Cost and field maintenance.
Recommended split: SBC for vision, MCU for barrier and sensors.

bank.q: Analyse how flooding and gossiping affect energy use and delay in a WSN. Propose a duty-cycling plan that improves network lifetime without losing coverage.
outline: Flooding sends to all neighbours and causes duplicates.
Gossiping sends to one or few neighbours and may be slow.
Energy cost of idle listening and retransmission.
Duty cycle with wake-up schedule.
Coverage check and cluster head rotation.

bank.q: A smart meter can use BLE, Zigbee or NB-IoT. Evaluate the three for range, data rate, power and security in an Indian apartment block.
outline: BLE range and phone pairing.
Zigbee mesh inside the building.
NB-IoT wide-area cellular link.
Power and battery life.
Security: pairing, keys, network access.

bank.q: Critique active RFID against QR codes for tracking costly construction equipment. Consider read range, line of sight, cost, battery and tamper risk.
outline: Active RFID long range and automatic reads.
QR needs line of sight and manual scan.
Tag cost and battery maintenance.
Tamper detection and durability.
Best fit for high-value movable assets.

bank.q: Explain why sensor drift, hysteresis and dead band can make a closed-loop actuator oscillate or settle with offset. Suggest calibration or control fixes.
outline: Drift shifts the measured value.
Hysteresis makes the loop response direction-dependent.
Dead band hides small errors.
Offset and limit cycles in control.
Fixes: calibration, filtering, dead-band compensation, better sensor.

glossary.def: Device that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
Element that converts one form of energy into another; a sensor is a transducer used for measurement.
How close a reading is to the true value.
How close repeated readings are to each other.
Change in output divided by change in input.
Smallest input change that gives a detectable output change.
Difference in output for the same input when approached from opposite directions.
Slow unwanted change in output at constant input.
Input interval with no output change.
Frequency range over which a sensor responds usefully.
Device that turns an electrical command into motion or force.
Motor plus feedback and controller for commanded position or speed.
Motor that moves in fixed steps for input pulses.
Permanent-magnet motor with electronic commutation.
Small device with sensing, compute, communication, power and identity.
WSN node with sensor, processor, radio and battery.
Node that collects data from a WSN and connects it to a network.
Processor that runs the device logic and interfaces sensors and actuators.
Radio or wired interface that carries data to and from the device.
Battery, mains supply or energy harvester that runs the device.
Single-chip computer with CPU, memory and input/output for control.
Full computer on one board with operating system and ports.
Network of small sensing nodes that relay data to a sink.
Clustering protocol that rotates cluster heads to save WSN energy.
Switching a node between sleep and active states to save power.
Radio-frequency identification; contactless reading of a tag identity.
